In [[geometry]], the '''Bevan point''', named after [[Benjamin Bevan]], is a [[triangle center]]. It is defined as center of the '''Bevan circle''', that is the circle through the centers of the three [[excircle]]s of a triangle.{{r|etc}}

The Bevan point of a triangle is the reflection of the [[incenter]] across the [[circumcenter]] of the triangle.{{r|etc}} Bevan posed the problem of proving this in 1804, in a mathematical problem column in ''The Mathematical Repository''.{{r|etc|mw}} The problem was solved in 1806 by John Butterworth.{{r|mw}}

The Bevan point {{mvar|M}} of triangle {{math|△''ABC''}} has the same distance from its [[Euler line]] {{mvar|e}} as its incenter {{mvar|I}}. Their distance is
<math display=block>\overline{MI} = 2\sqrt{R^2-\frac{abc}{a+b+c}} </math>
where {{mvar|R}} denotes the radius of the [[circumcircle]] and {{mvar|a, b, c}} the sides of {{math|△''ABC''}}.{{r|mw}}

The Bevan is point is also the midpoint of the line segment {{mvar|{{overline|NL}}}} connecting the [[Nagel point]] {{mvar|N}} and the [[de Longchamps point]] {{mvar|L}}.{{r|etc}} The radius of the Bevan circle is {{math|2''R''}}, that is twice the radius of the circumcircle.{{r|ctk}}
